title: Same-Origin Policy and CORS
summary: The browser isolates origins from each other by default, and CORS is the deliberate, server-controlled hole punched through that isolation — understanding the handshake is what turns a red console error into a five-minute fix.

slides.markdown:
Every frontend engineer eventually hits a red console error: **"has been blocked by CORS policy."** Most treat it as an obstacle to route around — adding a proxy, disabling security in dev — without understanding what it's actually protecting against.

The underlying rule is the **Same-Origin Policy (SOP)**: by default, script running on one origin cannot read responses from a different origin, full stop. **CORS** isn't a bypass of that rule — it's a protocol for the *server* to explicitly say "this other origin is allowed to read my responses," checked and enforced entirely by the browser.

This topic covers what an origin actually is, why SOP exists, the preflight handshake CORS runs to negotiate access, and how to actually read and fix a real CORS error instead of guessing at it.

slides.subTitle: Scheme + host + port
slides.markdown:
An origin is the exact triple **scheme + host + port**. All three must match for two URLs to be same-origin — this is stricter than most people assume:

- `https://example.com` and `http://example.com` — **different origins** (scheme differs).
- `https://example.com` and `https://api.example.com` — **different origins** (host differs; subdomains are not the same origin).
- `https://example.com` and `https://example.com:8443` — **different origins** (port differs).
- `https://example.com/page1` and `https://example.com/page2` — **same origin** (path is not part of the origin at all).

The subdomain case surprises people most: `app.example.com` and `api.example.com` are as cross-origin to each other as two completely unrelated domains, as far as SOP is concerned — sharing a parent domain grants nothing automatically.

Without SOP, visiting a malicious page would let its script make a request to `your-bank.com` — using **your logged-in cookies**, since the browser attaches them regardless of which tab initiated the request — and then **read the response**, extracting your account balance directly into the attacker's page.

That's the specific attack SOP prevents: it doesn't stop the request from being *sent* (that's a related but separate concern — CSRF), it stops the malicious script from **reading the response**. The request might still fire and even succeed server-side; SOP's guarantee is narrower and specific: your script can't see what came back from a different origin unless that origin opts in.

This is why SOP is a default-deny, opt-in-to-share model rather than an all-or-nothing block — the web genuinely needs cross-origin requests (loading a CDN's JS, calling a third-party API), so the platform needed a controlled way to say "yes, you may read this" rather than banning cross-origin requests outright.

Not every cross-origin request triggers the same CORS behavior. A **simple request** — `GET`/`POST`/`HEAD`, only a small allow-listed set of headers (`Accept`, `Accept-Language`, `Content-Type` limited to `text/plain`/`multipart/form-data`/`application/x-www-form-urlencoded`) — goes out immediately; the browser checks the *response*'s `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` and only then decides whether to expose the body to your script.

Anything else — a custom header like `Authorization`, `Content-Type: application/json`, or a method like `PUT`/`DELETE`/`PATCH` — is a **preflighted request**: the browser sends an `OPTIONS` request *first*, asking permission before sending the real one, and only proceeds with the actual request if the server's preflight response says yes.

This is the single most common source of confusion in CORS debugging: nearly every real JSON API call (`Content-Type: application/json`) is preflighted, meaning every such request costs an **extra round trip** the network tab shows as a separate `OPTIONS` entry that developers often don't recognize as related to their actual request at all.

For a preflighted request, the full exchange has two round trips before your data actually moves:

1. Browser sends `OPTIONS` with `Origin: https://app.example.com`, `Access-Control-Request-Method: PUT`, `Access-Control-Request-Headers: content-type`.
2. Server replies with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example.com`, `Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, PUT`, `Access-Control-Allow-Headers: content-type` — or omits these, implicitly denying.
3. If allowed, the browser sends the **actual** request, then checks the actual response's `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header again before handing the body to your JS.

slides.subTitle: Cookies plus CORS
slides.markdown:
By default, cross-origin `fetch`/`XHR` requests **don't send cookies** at all, even if the browser has them for that domain — you have to opt in explicitly with `credentials: 'include'`.

Once you do, the server has to opt in on its side too, with two specific requirements that trip people up:

- `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` must be present.
- `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` **cannot** be the wildcard `*` — it must be the exact requesting origin, echoed back.

This pairing exists because a wildcard `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` combined with credentials would mean *any* site on the internet could make a credentialed (cookie-carrying) request to your API and read the response — exactly the cross-origin data leak SOP exists to prevent. The browser enforces this combination as a hard rule; it isn't optional server configuration, it's a fetch spec requirement the browser itself checks and refuses to bypass.

slides.sectionTitle: Reading and fixing a real CORS error
slides.markdown:
A typical console error and how to actually diagnose it:

```text
Access to fetch at 'https://api.example.com/data' from origin
'https://app.example.com' has been blocked by CORS policy:
No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header is present on the
requested resource.
```

This is a **server-side** problem, not a client bug — no amount of client code changes it, because the browser is the one enforcing the block based on the response's headers. Steps that actually help:

1. Open the **Network tab**, find the request (it may be the `OPTIONS` preflight, not your actual call), and check the response headers directly — is `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` present at all? Does it match your exact origin?
2. If it's the preflight failing, check `Access-Control-Allow-Methods`/`-Headers` include what your actual request used.
3. Fix it on the **server**: add or correct the `Access-Control-Allow-*` headers for the specific origins that should be allowed.

A request that shows as "failed" in the console but returned real data in the Network tab is the tell-tale sign of a CORS block specifically — the server did respond, the browser just refused to expose it to your script.

slides.sectionTitle: CORS vs a proxy vs JSONP
slides.markdown:
Three ways teams have worked around cross-origin restrictions, with very different trade-offs:

| Approach | How it works | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| **CORS** | Server explicitly allows specific origins via headers | The correct, modern approach — explicit, auditable, works with credentials |
| **Server-side proxy** | Your own backend calls the third-party API and relays the response same-origin | Adds latency and infra, but total control over what's exposed; useful when you can't control the third-party's CORS headers at all |
| **JSONP (legacy)** | Abuses `<script src>` (which isn't subject to SOP) to load data as executable JS | No opt-in required from the target — and that's exactly the danger: it only works for GET, and it executes arbitrary code from that origin with no CORS-style verification at all |

JSONP predates CORS and is a real security liability by modern standards — it works precisely because `<script>` tags ignore SOP, meaning you're trusting the remote origin to not serve malicious JS, with no browser-enforced check at all. Treat any JSONP usage you encounter in an existing codebase as a migration target, not a pattern to add to.

A frequent "fix" for a CORS error is slapping `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` on every response, and it works — right up until credentials are involved, where the browser **actively refuses** to proceed, regardless of what the server sends.

```text
The value of the 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header in the response
must not be the wildcard '*' when the request's credentials mode is
'include'.
```

This isn't a server misconfiguration in the usual sense — it's the browser enforcing a fetch-spec rule that exists specifically because a wildcard-plus-credentials combination would let any origin on the internet read cookie-authenticated responses from your API. There's no server-side override; the fix is always the same: echo back the **specific requesting origin** (validated against an allow-list server-side) instead of a wildcard, whenever credentials are in play.

Teams sometimes discover this the hard way after wildcarding CORS in development (where credentials often aren't tested) and shipping to production where a logged-in user's request silently fails.

slides.sectionTitle: Where XSS and CSRF fit in
slides.markdown:
SOP and CORS are about **which origin can read which responses** — they're not the whole cross-origin security story. Two related but distinct concerns live one layer over, covered in depth in the `web-security` group:

- **CSRF** exploits the fact that SOP doesn't stop a request from being *sent*, only from being *read* — a forged cross-site form submission can still trigger a state-changing action using your cookies, even though the attacker's script can't see the response.
- **XSS** sidesteps SOP entirely by getting malicious script to run *inside* your own origin — at that point it's not "cross-origin" from the browser's perspective at all, so none of SOP's protections apply.

Knowing this boundary matters in interviews specifically because candidates often conflate all three under "cross-origin security" — SOP/CORS govern one specific thing (response readability across origins), and the other two are separate failure modes SOP was never designed to catch.

slides.sectionTitle: The cost of preflight, at scale
slides.markdown:
Preflight isn't just a debugging annoyance — it's a real, measurable latency cost at production scale. Every preflighted request (nearly every JSON API call) pays an extra round trip **before** the actual request even starts, on top of DNS/TCP/TLS setup for a cold connection.

The standard mitigation: `Access-Control-Max-Age` on the preflight response tells the browser to **cache** the preflight result for N seconds, so repeated calls to the same endpoint with the same method/headers skip the `OPTIONS` round trip entirely until the cache expires. Setting this to a sensible value (commonly hours, not seconds) is a legitimate, low-effort performance win for any API making frequent cross-origin calls — and one that's easy to overlook because the preflight itself is invisible unless you're specifically looking in the Network tab.

A repeatable diagnostic sequence, rather than trial-and-error header-adding:

1. **Is this actually a CORS error, or a network/server error mislabeled as one?** Check the Network tab — if the request shows a real response with data, it's CORS blocking JS from *reading* it, not a server failure.
2. **Simple or preflighted?** Custom headers, JSON content-type, or a non-simple method means look at the `OPTIONS` request first, not your actual call.
3. **Does the response include `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` matching your exact origin** (not a wildcard, if credentials are involved)?
4. **Are credentials in play?** If so, check both `credentials: 'include'` client-side and `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` plus a specific (non-wildcard) origin server-side.

Walking this sequence out loud in an interview — rather than jumping straight to "just add `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`" — is what signals you understand the mechanism instead of having memorized one fix that happens to work in the easy case.
